bullets: Game 6 of an 8-game single-deck session titled "#1 BEST Ronin Deck in Clash Royale"; a win in overtime against a top-ladder bridge-spam player running Hero Tombstone, Bandit, evolved Battle Ram, Musketeer, Skeleton Dragons, Heal Spirit and a Ronin of his own. His closing verdict at 1185s: "What a beautiful game, man. I love this deck so much."

The deck is piloted as defence-first chip, not as a push deck. Across the whole match the Ronin goes to the bridge exactly once (OT 1:18, tile [13, 14]) — every other Ronin is at rows 0-10 on his own half answering a Bandit or a Battle Ram — and that single bridge Ronin plus a Goblin Barrel takes the enemy right tower from 3665 to 330 HP in five seconds.

Cannon and Magic Archer carry the defence and are cycled aggressively: seven Cannons (rows 10-13, centre, so either lane can be pulled) and eight Magic Archers (rows 6-11, well behind the fight) in 277 s. "I need to keep cycling my magic archers, man. These magic archers like my saving grace" (OT 1:32) and "Look at this magic archer, guys. He's just absolutely untouchable" (OT 0:42).

Wall Breakers are a defensive card in this list as much as an offensive one — King-activation denial at clock 2:10 and 0:27, a Battle-Ram kite at 1:20 ("Let's just Wall Breakers to kite this away, so we don't have to defend the barbarian"), and a Bandit distraction at OT 0:38 — with bridge pairs saved for windows where the opponent is card-down.

The two spirits are a defensive package with a specific trick: dropped together in front of the King Tower at clock 1:10 they activate his own King on a crossing Bandit, which he calls the turning point — "Beautiful King activation. That's going to make defense a lot easier for the rest of the match" (1016-1019s). His king tower reads 7418 HP from t=1020 onward.

Skeletons are the deck's Ronin tech: surround the enemy Ronin so his parry is spent on a Skeleton, and drop them early — "you have to drop them a little bit early, it seems like, because if you don't drop them early, then obviously the Ronin will just hit [them] too quickly" (974-982s).

Offence is bait-shaped and lane-read driven: every Goblin Barrel goes to tile [14, 26] on the enemy right tower, chosen against where the opponent just committed ("Probably going to tombstone on the left so I'll go for the barrel on the right", OT 1:43) or ahead of a predicted spell ("He's probably going to go for the arrows here. So, I'm just going to go for the barrel now", OT 1:18), and the closer is the barrel and the runners together ("He's not going to be able to defend this goblin barrel plus wall breakers", OT 0:31).

new_deck.rationale: Goblin Barrel, Wall Breakers, Skeletons and both spirits all die to the same small spells, so one Log or Arrows can never cover the deck, and at 2.5 average elixir the threats come back around before the answer does — Ryley explicitly times a barrel against a predicted Arrows at OT 1:18.
new_deck.why_it_works_md: The list is built so that the two cheapest win conditions — Goblin Barrel and evolved Wall Breakers — bait the same small spell, while Ronin and Magic Archer do the actual defending. Ryley plays the Ronin almost entirely on his own half as a Bandit and Battle Ram answer, and cycles Magic Archers from rows 6-11 where nothing can reach them ("he's just absolutely untouchable", OT 0:42); the Cannon comes down on rotation rather than being held, which is what makes the deck stable against bridge spam. The spirit pair does double duty as reset and as a deliberate own-King-Tower activation — dropping Ice Spirit then Fire Spirit in front of the King at clock 1:10 turns three towers on to every subsequent push, which he calls the moment the match got easy. Damage then arrives in stacks the opponent cannot answer with one card: a bridge Ronin behind a Goblin Barrel when the opponent is card-down, or the barrel and the runners in the same second. Skeletons are the specific tech against the mirror — surround the enemy Ronin early so his parry is wasted.
